lessons.title: Encounter and Predict: The Cracked Frozen Bottle

quiz.prompt: A learner fills a 500 ml glass bottle to the brim with water, seals it with a metal cap and leaves it in a freezer overnight. In the morning the glass is cracked. Why did this surprise the class?
choices: Water cannot freeze when it is inside a sealed container
Freezers are not cold enough to freeze water
Glass is known to be the strongest material and should never crack
Everyday experience tells us that things usually shrink when they get cold, yet the water seemed to push the glass outwards
quiz.rationale: The puzzle is that the common idea 'things shrink when cooled' does not match the cracked glass. The other choices are not what the lesson identifies as the source of surprise.
quiz.placement: Predict card, stem (b): 'When things get cold, I think they generally… because…'

quiz.prompt: Learners studied a glass bottle that was filled to the brim with water, sealed with a metal cap and frozen overnight. Which of these is an OBSERVATION (something you can see) rather than an explanation?
choices: The glass shrank in the cold and squeezed the water until it cracked
The water heated up just before it froze and burst the bottle
A column of ice stuck out from the bottle where the cap had been
The metal cap rusted and weakened the glass
quiz.rationale: The protruding ice plug is direct evidence that can be seen on the specimen. The other choices are untested claims about why the bottle cracked.
quiz.placement: Observation Record: describe the crack pattern and the ice plug

quiz.prompt: The teacher said that in some places water left in a pipe, bucket or clay pot can freeze overnight and split its container. Which situation in Kenya is MOST likely to cause this?
choices: A rainy evening at 20°C in Kisumu
A hot afternoon at 32°C on the coast at Mombasa
A warm night at 28°C in Garissa
A night at 0°C or below in the highlands near the Aberdares or Mount Kenya
quiz.rationale: The Kenyan context bridge says that water freezes and splits containers where night temperatures fall to 0°C or below, such as the Aberdares, Mount Kenya slopes and Nyandarua.
quiz.placement: Kenyan Context Bridge: highland nights at or below 0°C

quiz.prompt: A learner predicts that a plastic bottle filled to the brim with water, sealed and frozen overnight would give a different result from a glass bottle. To test this prediction fairly, which set of conditions should be kept the same for both bottles?
choices: Same volume of water filled to the brim, same type of cap, and same time in the same freezer
One bottle in the freezer and the other left on the bench
Different amounts of water, because plastic is a different material
Only the colour of the bottles
quiz.rationale: A fair test changes only the bottle material. Water volume, filling, cap and freezing conditions must stay the same.
quiz.placement: Predict card, stem (c): plastic bottle instead of glass

quiz.prompt: After seeing the cracked bottle, which of these is the best INVESTIGABLE question, one the class could test with an experiment?
choices: Does a bottle that is only half-full of water crack less often than one filled to the brim?
Should learners be allowed to freeze bottles at home?
Who bought the bottle used in the demonstration?
Is glass prettier than plastic?
quiz.rationale: Changing how full the bottle is and observing whether it cracks can be tested. The other choices are opinions or facts that cannot be investigated by experiment.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: sticky-note questions about the cracked bottle

quiz.prompt: At the end of this first lesson, the class has seen the cracked bottle and heard the term 'anomalous expansion of water'. What is the status of the explanation for why the bottle cracked?
choices: The behaviour has been named and observed, but the full explanation will be investigated in later lessons
No one can ever explain it
It has been fully explained by the teacher, so there is nothing more to investigate
The cap was too tight, so that is the complete answer
quiz.rationale: This is an anchor lesson. The behaviour is named and the evidence is recorded, but the full explanation is deliberately left for the following lessons.
quiz.placement: Connect to phenomenon: naming 'anomalous expansion of water' on the DQB anchor strip

quiz.prompt: At the end of the lesson you draw a baseline model labelled 'MY MODEL — LESSON 1 (BEFORE INSTRUCTION)' showing what you think happens to the water in the sealed bottle overnight. What is the main purpose of this model?
choices: To get a mark for having the correct answer
To replace the Predict card, which can then be thrown away
To record your current ideas honestly, even if they are wrong, so you can compare and update them later in the unit
To copy the teacher's correct drawing
quiz.rationale: The teacher said the model 'does not have to be correct — it has to be honest'. It will be revised through the unit and compared with the final model.
quiz.placement: Baseline Particle Model: two-panel sketch signed and dated

lessons.title: Temperature Scales and Thermometers: Measuring the "How Hot"

quiz.prompt: A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a red alcohol column inside a thin glass tube. Why does the column rise when the bulb is placed in warm water?
choices: The alcohol expands as its temperature rises, so it moves up the narrow tube
The alcohol becomes heavier and sinks into the bulb
The alcohol evaporates and fills the tube with gas
The glass shrinks and squeezes the alcohol upwards
quiz.rationale: The thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the expansion of the liquid. The liquid expands with temperature and can only move up the narrow capillary tube.
quiz.placement: Station A: Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer

quiz.prompt: A clinical thermometer has a narrow kink (constriction) in the glass tube just above the bulb. What is the purpose of this constriction?
choices: It allows the thermometer to measure temperatures below 0 °C
It makes the liquid expand more quickly when it is heated
It stops the liquid column from falling back, so the reading stays after the thermometer is removed from the patient
It stops the liquid from expanding past 42 °C
quiz.rationale: The constriction holds the liquid column in place when the bulb cools, so the nurse can read the highest temperature reached.
quiz.placement: Station B: Clinical Thermometer (constriction as a design feature)

quiz.prompt: A bimetallic strip is made of brass bonded to iron. When it is heated, it bends so that the iron is on the inside of the curve and the brass is on the outside. What does this show?
choices: Brass and iron expand by exactly the same amount
Brass expands more than iron for the same temperature rise
Brass contracts while iron expands
Iron expands more than brass
quiz.rationale: The metal that expands more ends up on the outside of the curve. Brass is on the outside, so it expands more than iron.
quiz.placement: Station C: Bimetallic Strip teacher-supervised demo

quiz.prompt: What is a thermometric property?
choices: The unit printed on the scale of a thermometer
The material that a thermometer is made from
The lowest temperature that a thermometer can read
A physical property that changes continuously and reproducibly with temperature, such as the length of a liquid column
quiz.rationale: A thermometric property is any physical property that varies measurably and predictably with temperature. Examples are liquid expansion and the bending of a bimetallic strip.
quiz.placement: Teacher introduces THERMOMETRIC PROPERTY formally after the gallery debrief

quiz.prompt: The afternoon temperature in Marsabit peaks at 38 °C. What is this temperature in kelvin, using T(K) = T(°C) + 273?
quiz.placement: Kenyan weather data card: converting Marsabit 38 °C to Kelvin

quiz.prompt: A freezer runs at -18 °C. What is this temperature in kelvin, using T(K) = T(°C) + 273?
quiz.rationale: T(K) = -18 + 273 = 255 K. Adding 18 instead of subtracting it gives 291 K, which is a common error.
quiz.placement: Kenyan weather data card: converting the freezer -18 °C to Kelvin

quiz.prompt: On a hot afternoon in Kisumu, a thermometer calibrated in kelvin reads 300 K. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius, using T(K) = T(°C) + 273?
quiz.placement: Kenyan weather data card: Celsius–Kelvin conversions (Kelvin to Celsius)

quiz.prompt: A learner converts -18 °C to 255 K and says, "255 K is very close to absolute zero because it is a freezing temperature." Which response is correct?
choices: The learner is wrong, because 255 K is still 255 kelvin above absolute zero (0 K), which is a large difference
The learner is right, because absolute zero is -18 °C
The learner is wrong, because absolute zero is 255 K
The learner is right, because any temperature below 0 °C is close to absolute zero
quiz.rationale: Absolute zero is 0 K (about -273 °C). A freezer at 255 K is still far above it, so the particles still have a lot of kinetic energy.
quiz.placement: Q2 of the data card analysis: is 255 K close to absolute zero?

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what temperature tells us at the particle level?
choices: Temperature is the total amount of heat in a body, so a bucket of water at 30 °C has a higher temperature than a cup of water at 30 °C
Temperature is the number of particles in a body
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, so particles move faster at 291 K than at 255 K
Temperature is the size of the particles, which shrink as a body cools
quiz.rationale: Temperature relates to the average kinetic energy of the particles. A bucket and a cup at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy, even though the bucket holds more thermal energy.
quiz.placement: Q3 of the data card analysis: particle-level meaning of temperature (kinetic energy)

quiz.prompt: Water at Nairobi temperature (18 °C, which is 291 K) is cooled in a freezer at -18 °C (255 K). By how many kelvin does its temperature fall?
quiz.rationale: The temperature drop is 291 - 255 = 36 K. Equivalently, 18 - (-18) = 36 degrees, and a 1 °C change equals a 1 K change.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model revision: ΔT = -36 K annotation

lessons.title: Linear Expansion of Solids — The Stretching Rod

quiz.prompt: A 30 cm steel ruler is heated from 25 °C to 200 °C. Which prediction best matches what happens and why?
choices: It stays exactly the same length, because steel is too hard to change
It becomes slightly longer, because its particles vibrate more and the average distance between them increases
It becomes shorter, because the particles lose energy and move closer together
It becomes several centimetres longer, because heating makes the particles themselves bigger
quiz.rationale: Solids expand when heated because the particles vibrate with larger amplitude and the average spacing grows. For a 30 cm ruler the change is only a fraction of a millimetre, so the expansion is small and the particles do not change size.
quiz.placement: Predict: written prediction about the 30 cm metal ruler heated from 25 °C to 200 °C

quiz.prompt: In a bar-and-gauge experiment, a metal rod is heated and a dial gauge gives these readings: when the temperature rise ΔT is 10 °C, the length change ΔL is 0.1 mm; at 20 °C it is 0.2 mm; at 30 °C it is 0.3 mm; at 40 °C it is 0.4 mm. Which statement describes the pattern?
choices: ΔL changes randomly with no pattern
ΔL stays the same whatever the temperature rise
ΔL increases in proportion to ΔT: doubling the temperature rise doubles the length change
ΔL decreases as the temperature rise increases, so the rod shortens
quiz.rationale: Each time ΔT doubles, ΔL doubles (0.1 to 0.2 mm, 10 to 20 °C), so ΔL is directly proportional to ΔT. This is the pattern that leads to ΔL = αL₀ΔT.
quiz.placement: Observe: bar-and-gauge experiment, describing the relationship between ΔT and ΔL in the data table

quiz.prompt: The coefficient of linear expansivity (α) of a material is best described as:
choices: the total length change of any rod of that material, measured in metres
the fractional change in length per unit temperature rise, measured in K⁻¹
the length of a rod at 0 °C, measured in metres
the temperature at which a solid begins to expand, measured in K
quiz.rationale: From ΔL = αL₀ΔT, α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT). It is the change in length per unit original length per degree of temperature rise, so its SI unit is K⁻¹.
quiz.placement: Explain Part A: deriving ΔL = αL₀ΔT and defining α (units K⁻¹)

quiz.prompt: A steel bridge girder is 25 m long at a fitting temperature of 20 °C. In full sun its temperature reaches 65 °C. For steel, α = 11 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. By how much does the girder expand?
quiz.rationale: ΔT = 65 − 20 = 45 °C. ΔL = αL₀ΔT = 11 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 × 45 = 0.012375 m = 12.375 mm. Using 65 °C as ΔT gives the wrong value of 17.875 mm.
quiz.placement: Explain Part B: Bridge Girder Problem

quiz.prompt: A Kenya Power overhead aluminium cable near Kisumu is 200 m long at 15 °C. On a hot afternoon its temperature rises to 70 °C. For aluminium, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. What is the increase in length of the cable?
quiz.rationale: ΔT = 70 − 15 = 55 °C. ΔL = αL₀ΔT = 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 55 = 0.253 m, which is about 25 cm. Using 70 °C as ΔT gives the wrong value of 0.322 m.
quiz.placement: Explain Part C: Kenya Power Problem (homework), part (i)

quiz.prompt: Kenya Power overhead cables look more saggy on a hot afternoon than on a cool morning. Which explanation is correct, and why do engineers allow for the sag?
choices: The cable becomes longer when hot but the pylons stay fixed, so the extra length hangs down; engineers allow sag so the cable does not snap or damage the pylons when it contracts in cold weather
The cable gets heavier when hot, so it hangs lower; engineers allow sag to make the cable stronger
The cable contracts when hot and pulls the pylons together; engineers allow sag to save money on cable
The pylons expand much more than the cable, so the cable hangs lower; engineers allow sag so it is easier to repair
quiz.rationale: Heating lengthens the cable but the pylons stay the same distance apart, so the extra length forms a sag. A cable strung tight would be pulled very hard when it contracts in cool weather and could snap or damage the pylons.
quiz.placement: Explain Part C: Kenya Power Problem (homework), part (ii) explaining the sag

quiz.prompt: Railway engineers leave small gaps between lengths of steel rail. Suppose rails were laid end to end with no gaps on a very hot day in Kisumu. What would most likely happen?
choices: The rails would melt, because they gain energy from the sun
The rails would expand with nowhere to go, pushing on each other with large forces and buckling
The rails would stay exactly the same, because steel is too hard to expand
The rails would shrink and pull apart, because metals contract when hot
quiz.rationale: Steel expands when heated, so rails with no gaps push against each other with very large forces and buckle. This links to the cracked bottle, where expansion also produced forces large enough to damage a hard material.
quiz.placement: DQB: clustering evidence, Theme B 'Expansion forces can be large enough to damage structures'

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly explains, at particle level, why a metal rod gets longer when heated?
choices: New particles are added to the rod as it heats up
The particles move faster in straight lines through the rod, like gas particles, and push the ends outwards
The particles vibrate with larger amplitude about their positions, so the average distance between them increases
The particles themselves become bigger when heated
quiz.rationale: In a solid the particles stay in a lattice and vibrate. More heat means greater vibration amplitude and a larger average separation, so the rod lengthens. The particles stay the same size and are not moving freely like gas particles.
quiz.placement: Model: adding Panel 3 (linear expansion of a solid) to the cumulative particle model

lessons.title: Superficial and Volumetric Expansion — From Length to Volume

quiz.prompt: A 500 ml metal sufuria is filled to the brim with water at 20 °C and heated on a jiko to 80 °C. What happens to the volume of the water?
choices: It increases slightly, because water expands when heated in this temperature range
It stays the same, because the sufuria holds the water in
It decreases, because the water particles pack closer together when heated
It first decreases and then increases, because water is always densest at 20 °C
quiz.rationale: Water heated from 20 °C to 80 °C expands like most liquids. The unusual behaviour of water only occurs below 4 °C.
quiz.placement: Predict: Scenario A, sufuria heated on a jiko from 20 °C to 80 °C (bar graph prediction for 'Heating')

quiz.prompt: A square plate has side L₀. After heating, each side becomes L₀(1 + αΔT), so the new area is A = L₀²(1 + αΔT)². Why can we write A ≈ L₀²(1 + 2αΔT) and so say β ≈ 2α?
choices: Because the plate expands in only one direction when heated
Because the area of a square is always twice its side length
Because α is a very small number, so the (αΔT)² term is tiny and can be ignored
Because the (αΔT)² term is negative and cancels the 2αΔT term
quiz.rationale: Expanding gives 1 + 2αΔT + (αΔT)². Since α is about 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, (αΔT)² is extremely small compared with 2αΔT and can be dropped, so β ≈ 2α.
quiz.placement: Part A: Derivation Card, extending linear expansion to area and volume

quiz.prompt: A rectangular concrete bridge-deck slab is 12 m × 4 m at 15 °C. The linear expansivity of the concrete is α = 10 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. By how much does its area increase when it reaches 45 °C in the midday sun?
quiz.placement: Part A: bridge-deck slab problem (i), 12 m × 4 m slab heated from 15 °C to 45 °C

quiz.prompt: A 2-litre (2000 ml) aluminium sufuria has linear expansivity α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. It is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C. By how much does its internal volume increase?
quiz.rationale: γ = 3α = 69 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. ΔV = γV₀ΔT = 69 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 × 80 ≈ 11 ml. Using α or 2α instead of 3α gives the smaller wrong values.
quiz.placement: Part A: homework problem (ii), aluminium sufuria heated from 20 °C to 100 °C

quiz.prompt: A group cools a flask of water fitted with a narrow capillary tube. The water column height in the capillary is: 10 °C: 52 mm; 8 °C: 48 mm; 6 °C: 45 mm; 4 °C: 44 mm; 2 °C: 45 mm; 0 °C: 46 mm. At which temperature is the water densest?
choices: 10 °C, because the column is highest there
2 °C, because the column starts rising there
4 °C, because the column is lowest, so the volume is smallest
0 °C, because it is the coldest reading
quiz.rationale: The capillary column height shows volume. The lowest column (44 mm) means the smallest volume for the same mass, so the greatest density, at 4 °C. Below 4 °C the column rises again.
quiz.placement: Part B: Flask-and-Capillary Experiment, plotting Temperature vs. Capillary Height

quiz.prompt: A sealed glass bottle full of water cracks in a freezer. Which statement best explains the main cause of the crack?
choices: The water expands by about 9% when it freezes at 0 °C, and the sealed glass cannot stretch
The tiny expansion between 4 °C and 0 °C (about 0.01%) alone produces enough force to crack the glass
The glass contracts much more than the water when it gets cold
The water shrinks as it freezes and pulls the glass walls inwards
quiz.rationale: The main cause is the roughly 9% increase in volume when water changes state to ice at 0 °C. The 4 °C to 0 °C expansion is very small and is only the first sign of the unusual behaviour.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) frame, 'Why did the sealed bottle crack?'

quiz.prompt: Freezing increases the volume of water by about 9%. By how much does the volume increase when 500 ml of water freezes at 0 °C?
choices: 45 ml
545 ml
4.5 ml
9 ml
quiz.rationale: Increase = 9% of 500 ml = 0.09 × 500 = 45 ml, so the ice occupies about 545 ml. The formula ΔV = γV₀ΔT cannot be used because freezing is a change of state.
quiz.placement: Explain: scaffolded question 2, volume increase when 500 ml of water freezes at 0 °C

quiz.prompt: Why does ice take up more space than the same mass of liquid water?
choices: In ice the molecules sit in an open hexagonal lattice with larger gaps between them
Extra water molecules are added to the ice as it forms
The water molecules become larger when they freeze
In ice the molecules move faster and push each other apart
quiz.rationale: The number and size of the molecules do not change. In the hexagonal ice lattice the molecules are held in an open arrangement with greater spacing, so the same mass takes up more volume.
quiz.placement: Explain: scaffolded question 3, molecular diagram of ice hexagonal lattice

quiz.prompt: Which causal chain correctly explains why a sealed water bottle cracks in a freezer?
choices: Water freezes at 4 °C, becomes less dense than glass, and the metal cap pushes the glass until it cracks
Water cools to 4 °C and expands by 9%, then freezes and shrinks, the glass is pulled inwards and cracks
Water cools and keeps shrinking until it freezes, the glass shrinks more, the glass is squeezed and cracks
Water cools to 4 °C (smallest volume), then freezes at 0 °C and expands by about 9%, pressure on the glass rises above its tensile strength, and the glass cracks
quiz.rationale: Water reaches minimum volume at 4 °C, then expands, and expands by about 9% when it freezes at 0 °C. A sealed bottle cannot stretch, so the pressure rises above the tensile strength of the glass and it cracks.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: Zone B 'What EXPLAINS the crack' causal chain arrow card

lessons.title: Applications of Thermal Expansion: Engineering Solutions

quiz.prompt: An engineer is designing a long steel bridge in Kisumu, where the weather is hot for much of the year. What should the engineer build into the design so the beams do not push against their supports and crack?
choices: Small gaps or expansion joints at the ends of the beams
Beams made thicker so they cannot expand
Beams fixed tightly against the supports with no space
Steel painted a dark colour so it absorbs less heat
quiz.rationale: Steel lengthens when it warms, so the engineer leaves space (expansion joints) for the beam to expand. Fixing the beam tightly causes large forces, like the ice cracking the bottle.
quiz.placement: Predict: how might an engineer use the expansion formula to prevent damage to a long steel structure?

quiz.prompt: A bimetallic strip in an electric iron has brass bonded to invar steel. Brass expands more than invar for the same temperature rise. What happens to the strip when it is heated?
choices: It becomes shorter on both sides equally
It bends towards the brass side because brass becomes shorter
It bends towards the invar side because the brass lengthens more
It stays straight because the two metals cancel each other out
quiz.rationale: The brass lengthens more than the invar, so the brass side is on the outside of the curve and the strip bends towards the invar side. This bending breaks the circuit and switches the iron off.
quiz.placement: Observe: Card B - Bimetallic Strip Thermostat in an Electric Iron

quiz.prompt: A blacksmith heats a slightly undersized iron tyre before fitting it onto a wooden cart wheel, then cools it with water. Why does this make the tyre grip the wheel tightly?
choices: Heating makes the tyre expand so it slips over the wheel, and cooling makes it contract and squeeze the wheel
Water makes the wood swell, and this has nothing to do with the tyre
Heating makes the tyre shrink so it fits, and cooling makes it expand to grip the wheel
Heating melts the tyre so it takes the shape of the wheel
quiz.rationale: The hot tyre has a larger diameter so it slips on. As it cools it contracts back towards its original size and grips the wheel tightly.
quiz.placement: Observe: Card C - Fitting a Metal Tyre onto a Wooden Cart Wheel in Rural Kenya

quiz.prompt: Roofers in Kenya leave small gaps between neighbouring corrugated metal roofing sheets and use dome-headed rivets that allow slight movement. What is the engineering reason for this?
choices: To let rainwater drain between the sheets
To give the sheets room to expand in the afternoon heat so they do not buckle
To stop the sheets from expanding at all
To make the roof lighter
quiz.rationale: The sheets expand when heated by the sun. The gaps and movable rivets accommodate this expansion and prevent buckling. The engineer is accommodating expansion, not stopping it.
quiz.placement: Observe: Card D - Riveting Corrugated Metal Roofing Sheets

quiz.prompt: A steel bridge beam is 10 m long at 20 °C. The temperature in Kisumu rises by 15 °C. The linear expansivity of steel is 11 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. Using ΔL = αL₀ΔT, what is the total increase in length of the beam?
choices: 165 mm
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class worked example of the 10 m steel bridge beam in Kisumu

quiz.prompt: A Kenya Power copper cable is 200 m long at 15 °C. On a hot afternoon in Nairobi the temperature rises to 40 °C. The linear expansivity of copper is 17 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. By how much does the cable increase in length?
choices: 3.4 cm
136 cm
8.5 cm
quiz.rationale: The temperature rise is ΔT = 40 − 15 = 25 °C, not 40 °C. ΔL = αL₀ΔT = 17 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 25 = 0.085 m = 8.5 cm.
quiz.placement: Explain: independent parallel problem on the Kenya Power copper overhead cable

quiz.prompt: Why do engineers let overhead power cables sag between pylons instead of pulling them tight?
choices: The cable changes length with temperature, so the sag gives room for it to lengthen and shorten without being damaged
Sagging cables are cheaper because they use less metal
A tight cable would be too heavy for the pylons
Sagging cables carry more electric current
quiz.rationale: The metal expands in heat and contracts in cold. A cable pulled taut would be stretched or put under great force when it contracts. Sag allows for these length changes safely.
quiz.placement: Explain: independent copper cable problem - why engineers design the cable to sag

quiz.prompt: In a particle model of a steel beam heated on a hot day, which drawing best explains why the beam gets longer?
choices: The particles themselves become bigger
Particles stay bonded but vibrate with bigger amplitude, so their average spacing increases slightly
Particles stop moving and spread out evenly
Particles break away from each other and fly far apart
quiz.rationale: On heating, particles gain energy and vibrate more strongly about their fixed positions. Their average separation increases slightly, and this adds up to a small increase in the beam's length. The particles do not fly apart.
quiz.placement: Model: Lesson 5 panel - Engineering Response to Expansion (bridge beam cold and hot)

quiz.prompt: Which statement best links the cracked frozen bottle to the expansion gaps in a bridge?
choices: Expansion gaps are needed only because steel expands more than water
Expansion only causes damage in liquids, never in solid steel
Expansion that has nowhere to go produces a very large force, so engineers leave gaps to allow for it
Bridges and bottles are both damaged only when they get cold
quiz.rationale: When expansion is contained, as with ice in the bottle, it creates huge forces. Engineers use ΔL = αL₀ΔT to leave gaps that give the expansion room and avoid damage.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: Engineering Solutions column - 'Engineers use the expansion formula to ___'

lessons.title: Model Revision, Synthesis, and DQB Resolution — Explaining the Crack

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 learner fills a glass bottle to the brim with water, seals it with a metal cap and leaves it in a freezer overnight. The bottle cracks. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The water molecules arranged into an open hexagonal lattice with more spacing, so the water gained about 9% in volume and pushed outwards on the glass.
The cold air in the freezer pushed inwards on the glass until it cracked.
The water molecules became larger when they were cooled, so the water took up more space.
The glass shrank in the cold more than the water did, so the water was squeezed out.
quiz.rationale: Hydrogen bonding locks water molecules into a hexagonal lattice with greater spacing, so freezing increases the volume by about 9%. This pushes outwards on the glass. The molecules do not get bigger, and cold air does not push the glass in.
quiz.placement: Then vs. Now statements and the LESSON 1 MODEL | FINAL MODEL T-chart

quiz.prompt: A home freezer is set at -18 °C. Using T(K) = T(°C) + 273, what is this temperature on the Kelvin scale?
quiz.rationale: T(K) = -18 + 273 = 255 K. Kelvin values are never negative here, and adding 18 instead of subtracting gives the wrong answer of 291 K.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk, Station 1: Temperature Scales

quiz.prompt: A steel bridge girder is 25 m long. Its temperature rises by 45 °C. The expansion coefficient of steel is 11 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. Using ΔL = αL₀ΔT, by how much does the girder lengthen?
choices: 124 mm
275 mm
quiz.rationale: ΔL = 11 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 × 45 = 0.012375 m, which is about 12.4 mm. The other values come from wrong powers of ten or from leaving out 10⁻⁶ and ΔT.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk, Station 3: Linear Expansion of Solids (steel bridge girder)

quiz.prompt: Water increases in volume by about 9% when it freezes at 0 °C. A bottle is completely full with 500 ml of water. By about how much does the volume increase when all the water freezes?
choices: 9 ml
450 ml
4.5 ml
45 ml
quiz.rationale: 9% of 500 ml = (9 ÷ 100) × 500 = 45 ml, so the ice takes up about 545 ml.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk, Station 4: Volume Expansion (500 ml becomes about 545 ml)

quiz.prompt: A beaker of water at 10 °C is cooled slowly down to 0 °C. How does the density of the water change?
choices: It increases until 4 °C and then decreases as it cools towards 0 °C.
It increases all the way from 10 °C to 0 °C, like most liquids.
It decreases all the way from 10 °C to 0 °C.
It stays the same, because water does not change volume when cooled.
quiz.rationale: Water has its maximum density at 4 °C. Below 4 °C it expands as it cools, which is why water is anomalous. Most liquids keep getting denser as they cool.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk, Station 5: Anomalous Expansion of Water (density vs. temperature graph)

quiz.prompt: A bottle completely full of water and tightly sealed cracks in a freezer. Why does the expanding water crack the glass instead of simply pushing the cap off or fitting inside?
choices: Ice is lighter than water, so it floats up and hits the cap.
Glass always becomes brittle at 0 °C and breaks by itself, with or without water.
The ice pulls the glass walls inwards until they snap.
The rigid, sealed, full bottle gives the expanding ice no room to grow, so it presses very hard outwards on the glass walls.
quiz.rationale: Water expands by about 9% on freezing. A rigid, sealed and completely full bottle cannot make room for this, so a large outward pressure acts on the glass and can exceed its tensile strength.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation Poster, Section C: The Quantitative Explanation

quiz.prompt: Why do the molecules in ice have greater spacing than the molecules in liquid water?
choices: Ice molecules move faster than liquid molecules, so they spread apart.
Hydrogen bonding holds the molecules in an open hexagonal lattice with greater spacing.
Air bubbles trapped between the molecules push them apart.
Freezing makes each water molecule bigger.
quiz.rationale: Hydrogen bonds fix each water molecule in a hexagonal lattice with large gaps, so ice is less dense than liquid water. Molecules in ice vibrate less, not more, and the molecules do not grow.
quiz.placement: Final revision of the cumulative particle model (ice at 0 °C, hexagonal lattice with greater intermolecular spacing)

quiz.prompt: A learner asks: "Why can we not use ΔV = γV₀ΔT to work out the 9% volume increase when water freezes at 0 °C?" What is the best answer?
choices: The formula only works for temperatures above 100 °C.
The formula gives the wrong answer because water does not expand when it freezes.
The formula only works for gases and never for liquids.
Freezing is a phase change with its own volume increase of about 9%, while the formula describes expansion within one phase.
quiz.rationale: ΔV = γV₀ΔT describes ordinary heating or cooling within a single phase, such as the aluminium sufuria. The 9% increase on freezing is a phase-change effect caused by the open ice lattice.

quiz.prompt: Farmers in the Nyandarua highlands cover their water pipes with insulation in January. What is the main scientific reason?
choices: Insulation makes the pipe metal expand so that it fits the water better.
Insulation turns the water into steam, which cannot damage the pipe.
Cold makes water contract, and the shrinking water pulls the pipe walls inwards.
Insulation stops the water in the pipes from freezing, because ice takes up about 9% more volume and can burst the pipe.
quiz.rationale: If water freezes inside a pipe it expands by about 9%, just like in the bottle, and the pressure can burst the pipe. Insulation helps keep the water above freezing.
